浪人.note: Langren renders the Japanese rōnin, a masterless samurai; by extension a rootless adventurer or tough. In these essays it means Japanese hoodlums and adventurers in the treaty ports.

空頭支票.note: Literally an “empty-head check”: a check drawn on an account with no funds to cover it. The modern English idiom carries the sense.

本票.note: A note a native bank (qianzhuang) issues drawn on itself, as against a depositor’s check drawn on his own account.

角子.note: The Shanghai word for the small silver subsidiary coins—the ten-cent and twenty-cent pieces, a tenth and a fifth of a dollar.

陳長庚.note: An actress of the Shanghai all-girl opera houses, as the author names her.

紅菊花.note: An actress of the all-girl opera houses; the stage name means “Red Chrysanthemum.”

恩曉峰.note: En Xiaofeng (1887–1949), a Manchu of Beijing and one of the celebrated female laosheng (bearded-old-man-role) singers of Peking opera’s early all-women stage.

張文奎.note: An actress of the Dangui all-girl house, as the author names her.

張文豔.note: An actress of the Dangui all-girl house, as the author names her.

白玉梅.note: An actress of the Dangui all-girl house, as the author names her.

張少泉.note: An actress of the Dangui all-girl house, as the author names her.

牛桂芬.note: An actress of the Dangui all-girl house, as the author names her.

胡家宅.note: A locality off Fourth Avenue (Fuzhou Road) in the Settlement, as the author places it.

寶善街.note: An old entertainment street in the Settlement, near Fourth Avenue.

大新街.note: A street in the old Shanghai amusement quarter.

寧波路.note: An east-west street of the International Settlement.

天津路.note: An east-west street of the International Settlement, parallel to Ningbo Road.

妙舞臺.note: An all-girl theater in Nanshi, on the old site of the New Stage.

大富貴.note: An all-girl theater on Daxin Street; the name means “Great Wealth and Rank.”

丹桂.note: An all-girl theater on Baoshan Street named here; a celebrated Dangui First Stage (丹桂第一台) on Fuzhou Road appears earlier in the book, and the two houses shared the name.

ch156.anchor: a way of owning the fault and clearing away the quarrel
ch156.note: A face-saving reconciliation ritual: the party in the wrong is sent by a go-between to burn incense and candles (and sometimes let off a string of firecrackers) at the house or shop of the party he has offended, as a public admission of fault that closes the quarrel.

ch157.anchor: another name for a vagrant with no honest occupation
ch157.note: Langren renders the Japanese rōnin, a masterless samurai; by extension a rootless adventurer or tough. Here it means the Japanese hoodlums and adventurers who congregated in the treaty ports.

ch157.anchor: the ronin's native soil lies for the most part in a certain country
ch157.note: “A certain country” (某國) is the author’s euphemism for Japan. The reprint prints the phrase in full rather than blanking it as ××; two essays on, in “Counterfeit Banknotes,” he drops the veil and names 日本 (Japan) outright.

ch157.anchor: secretly printing the banned old-calendar almanac
ch157.note: Under the Republic the government promoted the Western (Gregorian) calendar and restricted the old lunar almanac (舊曆/通書); printing it was an offense, so a black-market trade in the banned almanac grew up. On the calendar politics see the notes at the New-Year essay and the fortune-teller’s almanac.

The “January 28th” (一二八) is the Shanghai Incident of 28 January 1932, when Japanese forces attacked Zhabei and the districts north of the Settlement; the Chinese 19th Route Army resisted for over a month before withdrawing in March. Hongkou, named just below, was the de facto Japanese quarter of Shanghai (see the earlier notes on Hongkou). Corroborated by the standard histories.

ch158.anchor: no one knows the sense of it
ch158.note: The inversion recalls the New-Year custom of pasting the character 福 (“fortune”) upside down, a pun on dao (倒, “upside down”) and dao (到, “to arrive”), so that “fortune upside down” reads “fortune arrives.” What an inverted 火 (“fire”) was meant to signify is obscure; the author records the puzzle rather than inventing an answer.

ch159.anchor: do not really mean that a tree will bloom
ch159.note: Shu shang kai hua, “flowers on the tree,” is one of the classic Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六計), the art of making a paltry force look imposing by borrowed display. In Shanghai cant it was borrowed for the contingency-fee arrangement described here, where the doer of a job is paid only out of the winnings.

ch160.anchor: such contraband as raw opium, opium pellets, morphine, or huahui lottery slips
ch160.note: Yantu (raw opium), yanpao (prepared opium pellets ready for the pipe), and mafei (morphine) are graduated forms of the drug; huahui slips are betting tickets for the huahui lottery (glossed earlier). On the opium and morphine trade see the earlier notes.

ch161.anchor: writing out rubber checks by the score to work their swindles
ch161.note: A “rubber check” renders kongtou zhipiao, literally an “empty-head check”—one drawn on an account with no funds to cover it. The modern English idiom carries the sense.

ch161.anchor: the note a native bank draws on itself is called a cashier's note
ch161.note: A benpiao (cashier’s note, or promissory note) is a note a native bank issues drawn on itself, as against a depositor’s check drawn on his own account; a forged one is put out by a sham bank with nothing behind it.

ch161.anchor: a native bank run on the Empty-Fort ploy
ch161.note: The Empty-Fort ploy (空城計): Zhuge Liang’s ruse of flinging open the gates of an undefended city to bluff a wary enemy into retreat—all imposing front and no substance. See the fuller note where the stratagem first appears.

ch162.anchor: nine in ten have had a Japanese ronin playing a leading part within
ch162.note: Here the author names 日本浪人 (Japanese ronin) outright, dropping the “a certain country” (某國) euphemism he used two essays earlier; the barb about “good-neighborliness and benevolence” mocks Japan’s professed friendship toward China.

ch162.anchor: the subsidiary-currency notes put out by the central banks
ch162.note: Fubi is subsidiary or fractional currency—the small denominations below the dollar; the “jiao notes” (角票) are paper notes for tenths of a dollar. See the following essays on counterfeit small coin.

ch163.anchor: one must lose the agio besides
ch163.note: Tieshui, the agio: the make-weight premium charged when exchanging coin of light or doubtful weight for full-value money, so that an underweight dollar fetches less than its face.

ch164.note: Jiaozi, “jiao pieces,” is the Shanghai word for the small silver subsidiary coins—the ten-cent and twenty-cent pieces, a tenth and a fifth of a dollar. On the money system see the earlier notes.

A yanzhi dian, “tobacco-and-paper shop,” is the ubiquitous little Shanghai sundries shop selling cigarettes, joss paper, matches, stationery and small change—a natural clearing-house for coin, good or bad.

ch165.anchor: a real connoisseur, an expert in bronze and stone
ch165.note: Jinshi, “metal and stone,” is the study of ancient inscriptions on bronze vessels and stone stelae—the epigrapher’s connoisseurship by which old seals, scripts and papers are authenticated.

ch165.anchor: the shop has a byword that runs
ch165.note: A fan shop (扇子店) sold folding fans and painted fan-leaves and dealt in calligraphy and painting; its slogan bao zhen bu bao hao (“genuine guaranteed, good not guaranteed”) warrants only that a piece is really by the named hand, not that it is a fine example. On the mounting-shop trade in old scrolls see the earlier essay.

ch166.anchor: their faces are as red as Lord Guan's
ch166.note: Lord Guan (關公) is Guan Yu, the general of the Three Kingdoms deified as the god of war and loyalty; his image is always painted with a deep-red face, so a flushed, drunken face is “red as Lord Guan’s.”

ch167.note: Maoer xi, the all-girl opera: theaters staffed wholly by female performers, originally young girls (maoer, “the young ones”). They flourished in late-Qing and early-Republican Shanghai—the more so after the Beijing government banned mixed-sex casts in 1913, forcing women into all-female troupes—and died out once men and women were again allowed to act together.

ch167.anchor: all sang there in their day
ch167.note: Kunjue (坤角) means a female performer (kun, the female principle); these were the star actresses of the all-girl houses. Lin Daiyu here is the celebrated Shanghai courtesan-performer who took that stage name, not the Dream of the Red Chamber heroine (see the earlier note); En Xiaofeng, named just below, was a noted female laosheng.

ch167.anchor: ever since the fashion for men and women acting together came in
ch167.note: For much of the Qing and early Republic mixed-sex casts were forbidden and troupes were all-male or all-female; the Beijing government reaffirmed the ban in 1913. When it gave way in the 1920s and 1930s and men and women could act together, the all-girl houses lost their reason for being.
